To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
screen-time and unhealthy behaviours cluster in young children and parents’ own unhealthy behaviours are important influencing factors.
Screen-time (ST) and unhealthy dietary behaviours co-occur in children as young at age 5 years.
Screen-time and unhealthy dietary behaviour patterns cluster in 5–6-year-old children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of behavioural patterns in children and how they are influenced by the home environment.
understanding and addressing the complex nature of the relationship between screen-time, unhealthy dietary behaviours, and the physical environment.
the identification of the correlates of unhealthy behaviours in young children, and the development of interventions to promote healthy lifestyles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study provides evidence of the importance of parental modelling and the home environment on children’s screen time and dietary behaviours, with a need for further research in this area.
the clustering of screen and unhealthy eating behaviours in children is a serious public health issue that warrants further research.
the results of the current study are not conclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that screen-time and unhealthy behaviours cluster and are associated with sociodemographic factors, parental behaviours, and home physical environments.

the clustering of unhealthy behaviours, including screen-time and unhealthy diets, in young children is influenced by parental income, parental screen-time and unhealthy diet behaviours, and home food availability.
there are a number of factors that are associated with unhealthy dietary and screen time behaviours in young children, and that these factors are often inter-related.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to consider the clustering of multiple health risk behaviours when designing interventions for young children and to consider the influence of parents on their children’s behaviours.
we can no longer consider the health behaviours of children as independent of each other.
it is important to consider multiple behaviours when designing interventions to promote health in young children.
